```{r, results='hide'}
socioeconomic_index_raw <- read_csv("bc_sei_data_raw.csv")
```

# Cleaning

Let's get a sense of the data here.

```{r}
head(socioeconomic_index_raw)
```

First, I will get rid of columns that I do not need.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- socioeconomic_index_raw |>
  select(-CALENDAR_YEAR)
```

Now, I will only include the municipalities of interest.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  filter(
    MUN_NAME_2021 %in% c(
    "Anmore", "Belcarra", "Bowen Island", "Burnaby",
    "Coquitlam", "Delta", "Langley", "Lions Bay", "Maple Ridge", 
    "Metro Vancouver A", "New Westminster", "North Vancouver", 
    "Pitt Meadows", "Port Coquitlam", "Port Moody", "Richmond",
    "Surrey", "Vancouver", "West Vancouver", "White Rock", "Central Saanich",
    "Colwood", "Esquimalt", "Highlands", "Juan de Fuca (Part 1)", 
    "Juan de Fuca (Part 2)", "Langford", "Metchosin", "North Saanich",
    "Oak Bay", "Saanich", "Sidney", "Sooke", "Victoria", "View Royal"
  )
)
```

In the dataset, some municipalities are named twice because they contain
sub-regions or districts. It is important that we give these better
identifiers so that we can be more precise in our analysis.

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    MUN_NAME_2021 = case_when(
    CSD_UID == "5915002" ~ "City of Langley",
    CSD_UID == "5915001" ~ "Township of Langley",
    CSD_UID == "5915020" ~ "Electoral Area A (UBC)",
    CSD_UID == "5915051" ~ "City of North Vancouver",
    CSD_UID == "5915046" ~ "District of North Vancouver",
    CSD_UID == "5917054" ~ "Juan de Fuca (Part 1, Shirley, Jordan River, Malahat)",
    CSD_UID == "5917056" ~ "Juan de Fuca (Part 2, Port Renfrew)",
    TRUE ~ MUN_NAME_2021
  )
)
```

Let's also rename the columns

```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  rename(
    Municipality = MUN_NAME_2021,
    Average_Age = AVERAGE_AGE,
    Population_2023 = POPULATION_ESTIMATE,
    Total_Index = TOTAL_INDEX_0_100,
    Socioeconomic_Index = SEI_INDEX_0_100,
    Economics = ECON_0_100,
    Education = EDUC_0_100,
    Health = HEALTH_0_100,
    Community = COMMUNITY_0_100
  )
```

Now, lets make it so that the index data only goes up to two decminal
points.

```{r}
#| warning: false

index_decimal <- 2

cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        Total_Index, 
        Socioeconomic_Index, 
        Economics,
        Education,
        Health, 
        Community
    ), 
    round, digits = index_decimal
  )
)

cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  as_tibble()
```

I also want to make the age variable an interger without decimal points.

```{r}
age_decimal <- 0

cleaned_socioeconomic_index <- cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        Average_Age
      ),
      round, digits = age_decimal
  )
)

cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  as_tibble()
```

# Tests

I have two basic tests I want to run. 
The first is to make sure all variables are proper class. I am
doing this by using the stopifnot function, which will stop running the
code if it detects a variable that is not the proper class. The second
is to make sure there are no negative values in the numeric variables.
This code uses a logical if/else function to print out either 'passed' or 'stop'
statements depending on whether number less than zero are found in each
variable.

```{r}
stopifnot(
  "Municipality must be a character" = is.character(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Municipality),
  "Population must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Population_2023),
  "Average age must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Average_Age),
  "Total index must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Total_Index),
  "SEI Index muste be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Socioeconomic_Index),
  "Community must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Community),
  "Health must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Health),
  "Education must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Education),
  "Economics must be numeric" = is.numeric(cleaned_socioeconomic_index$Economics)
)
```

```{r}
numeric_variables <- c(
  "Population_2023", "Average_Age", "Total_Index", "Socioeconomic_Index",
  "Community", "Health", "Education", "Economics"
)

for(
  SEI_var in numeric_variables) {
    if(any(cleaned_socioeconomic_index[[SEI_var]] < 0, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      stop(
        paste("Stop, there are negative values in the", SEI_var, "variable"))
 } else {
      message(
        paste("Passed, there are no negative values in the", SEI_var, "variable") 
  )
 }
}
```

Looks like all the tests passed and there are no negative numbers where
there should not be.

## Bar Graphs

First, I want to create a bar graph that shows SEI score by each municipality. I
also reordered the municipalities so that they are ordered from highest SEI score
to lowest SEI score. I create a new variable that encapsulates all
the municipalities in Metro Vancouver. Then, I use a logical if_else
function to mutate the dataset so that the rest of the municipalities 
not included in Metro Vancouver are placed in the CRD.

```{r}
metro_vancouver <- c(
  "Anmore", "Belcarra", "Bowen Island", "Burnaby", "City of Langley",
  "City of North Vancouver", "Coquitlam", "Delta", "District of North Vancouver",
  "Electoral Area A (UBC)", "Lions Bay", "Maple Ridge", "New Westminister",
  "Pitt Meadows", "Port Coquitlam", "Port Moody", "Richmond", "Surrey",
  "Township of Langley", "Vancouver", "West Vancouver", "White Rock"
)

cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      Municipality %in% metro_vancouver, "Metro Vancouver", "Capital Regional District"
      ),
    Municipality = reorder(Municipality, Socioeconomic_Index)
      ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = Municipality, y = Socioeconomic_Index, fill = Region
      )
    ) +
      geom_col(
        colour = "black", width = 0.5
    ) +
      coord_flip() +
      scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("Metro Vancouver" = "skyblue", "Capital Regional District" =
        "forestgreen")
      ) +
      labs(
        title = "SEI Score by Municipality: Metro Vancouver & Greater Victoria",
        x = "Municipality",
        y = "SEI Score",
        fill = "Region"
    ) +
      theme_minimal(
        base_size = 8
    ) +
      theme(
        legend.position = "bottom"
      )
```

Alternatively, here is a bar graph that separates SEI scores by metropolitan
region. This gives us an interesting peek into well-being index scores by
metropolitan region.

```{r}
metro_vancouver <- c(
  "Anmore", "Belcarra", "Bowen Island", "Burnaby", "City of Langley",
  "City of North Vancouver", "Coquitlam", "Delta", "District of North Vancouver",
  "Electoral Area A (UBC)", "Lions Bay", "Maple Ridge", "New Westminister",
  "Pitt Meadows", "Port Coquitlam", "Port Moody", "Richmond", "Surrey",
  "Township of Langley", "Vancouver", "West Vancouver", "White Rock"
)

cleaned_socioeconomic_index |>
  mutate(
    Region = if_else(
      Municipality %in% metro_vancouver, "Metro Vancouver", "Capital Regional District"
      ),
    Municipality = reorder(Municipality, Socioeconomic_Index)
      ) |>
    ggplot(
      aes(
        x = Municipality, y = Socioeconomic_Index
        )
      ) +
      geom_col(
        fill = "lavender", colour = "black", width = 0.5
      ) +
      coord_flip(
      ) +
      facet_grid(
        Region ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free"
      ) +
      labs(
        title = "Comparing SEI Index By Metropolitan Region",
        x = "Metropolitan Region",
        y = "SEI Index"
      ) +
      theme_minimal(
        base_size = 8
      )
```

Based on this graph, we can see that SEI index scores are relatively higher 
in the Metro Vancouver region than the CRD. 

## Box Plot

Lastly, we can create a box plot to see the distribution of scores across key
numeric variables in my dataset. We will look at education, heath, community,
economics, and SEI index. 

First, I am going to use the pivot_longer function 
to reshape my data, the names_to argument makes a new column at the end of the 
dataset and names each dimension (Education, Heath, etc...) in this new column 
for each municipality. The values_to argument prints the scores to each 
respective dimension into a new column. The reason I am reshaping the data is 
because it makes it easier for ggplot to differentiate each dimension. It 
creates five separate rows for each municipality, instead of each municiaplity 
only having one row containing all five dimensions.


```{r}
cleaned_socioeconomic_index |> 
  pivot_longer(
    c(
      Education, Health, Community, Economics, Socioeconomic_Index
      ),
    names_to = "Wellbeing_Dimension",
    values_to = "Score"
    ) |>

ggplot(
  aes(
    x = Wellbeing_Dimension, y = Score, fill = Wellbeing_Dimension
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = 0.7, width = 0.5, outlier.color = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Health, Education, Community, Economics, and SEI Scores",
    x = "Index Dimension",
    y = "Score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(
    base_size = 6
  )
  
```
Based on this graph, we can see that economics has the highest median index score,
while health has the lowest. The median SEI index is floating around a score of 55
out of 100. It also seems that education has the largest variability within
the 25th and 75th percentile and community has the lowest variability within
the 25th and 75th percentile.
